paras: The killing of Mike Tillman took place on November 29, 1888, Thanksgiving Day, in Yamacraw, a Black quarter of Savannah, Georgia, when Patrolman Pat McMurray shot Tillman, a Black man he had arrested, during a struggle over the officer's club. Tillman died that evening, and the shooting set off a crowd attack in which McMurray, a second patrolman and a white laborer were beaten unconscious. Newspapers across the country reported the episode as a "negro riot", while a coroner's jury found Tillman killed by "party or parties unknown" over the dissent of its three Black members.
Yamacraw was described as a "negro quarter" of the city, where the holiday left, in the Marietta Journal's words, "many idle hands".

According to McMurray's statement to the Morning News, shortly before noon on Farm street he arrested a man who had cursed him, and a crowd quickly surrounded them. He said the man wrenched his club away, struck him twice over the head and seized his revolver, which McMurray wrenched back before he began shooting. The man ran down Farm street toward Orange with the officer firing after him, was caught on a stoop where a door was shut against him, and fell, saying he was dying.

When McMurray went back for his helmet, a crowd the Morning News put at 300 or 400 men and women attacked him with sticks, rocks and clubs. He fled into a house kept by Pearl Prendergast, but the crowd broke in, dragged him into the street and beat him insensible, shouting, by the paper's account, "We want justice!" and "He killed the man for nothing!" Nearby, Patrolman Daniel J. Cronin was beaten unconscious, and John Crimmens, a worker who went to his aid, was stabbed.
Tillman was carried to his mother's home on Lumber street, where Dr. B. F. Sheftall found eight bullet holes in his lower abdomen and thighs, and he died shortly afterward.

At Coroner Dixon's inquest on November 30, witnesses were "almost impossible" to secure among Black residents of the neighborhood. Dr. Sheftall testified that four shots made the eight holes, and one witness saw no interference by the crowd during the fight for the club. The jury of nine white and three Black men found that Tillman died of pistol wounds "held in the hands of party or parties unknown while engaged in riotous conduct", and the three Black jurors signed their disagreement.

Police arrested about thirty-six Black residents, while white residents raised funds for the three wounded men and for Mrs. Quinn, the wife of a patrolman who had held the crowd back with a revolver. On December 21 a grand jury indicted sixteen Black men and one Black woman for assault with intent to murder Cronin, Dan Henderson was convicted of the same charge against McMurray, and Joe Cotton's trial was under way. No report of any charge or further inquiry against McMurray appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News covered the episode at length under the headline "Beaten by a Mad Mob: One Thousand Negroes Run Riot in Yamacraw", called Tillman "one of the negro rioters", and wrote that McMurray was "supposed to have shot" him. Outside Savannah, Tillman went unnamed, and the New York Sun headlined "A Negro Riot Quelled", blamed whiskey, and said the crowd acted "with the ferocity of savages". Wire versions printed on November 30 in Omaha, Sacramento and Wilmington, Delaware, led with the injured officers, one noting only at its end that a negro with seven bullet wounds had been found dead. The Marietta Journal wrote that the crowd "acted more like demons than human beings", and a special in the Huntsville Gazette claimed that Cronin (spelled "Crohan") had killed a Black man in an arrest four months earlier and was "marked for slaughter".

Every account of the shooting comes from McMurray or the white press, and they differ: in his statement he wrenched back his pistol before firing, while the Morning News narrative has him knocked down and firing as the man stood over him. Against the officer's account stood the crowd's cry that he "killed the man for nothing" and the dissent of the three Black coroner's jurors.

accounts.label: McMurray's statement
accounts.gist: He arrested a man who cursed him; the man wrenched away his club, struck him twice and grabbed his revolver; McMurray wrenched the pistol back, began shooting, and pursued him firing until he was captured on a stoop.

accounts.label: Morning News narrative
accounts.gist: A crowd of the arrested man's friends knocked McMurray down, and he fired as the arrested man stood over him with the club.

accounts.label: Wire reports
accounts.gist: McMurray, set upon while dispersing a disorderly crowd, drew his revolver and fired; one wire version has him shoot the man wielding the club and fire four more balls into him as he ran.

accounts.label: The crowd
accounts.gist: As reported by the Morning News, the crowd shouted that it wanted justice and that McMurray 'killed the man for nothing.'

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Tillman died of pistol wounds from 'party or parties unknown while engaged in riotous conduct'; the three colored jurors signed in disagreement.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headlined 'Beaten by a Mad Mob: One Thousand Negroes Run Riot in Yamacraw', called Tillman 'one of the negro rioters' and praised the officers and their rescuers.
The New York Sun headlined 'A Negro Riot Quelled', blamed whiskey, and said the crowd acted 'with the ferocity of savages'.
Wire versions in the Omaha Bee, Sacramento Record-Union and Wilmington Evening Journal led with the injured officers and mentioned the dead man briefly, unnamed.
The Marietta Journal said the crowd 'acted more like demons than human beings' and blamed the holiday, drink and the women.
The Huntsville Gazette's short special described an arrest resisted by a crowd and added that Crohan had killed a negro four months before and was 'marked for slaughter'.
